section_1.title: The Foundation: Bernoulli Trials
section_1.content: Introduce prerequisite knowledge: The Bernoulli trial. Explain that a Binomial distribution is simply a series of these independent 'Yes/No' trials. Use a visual of a light switch (On/Off) or a coin toss.
section_1.example: Meet 'Finn the Frog'. Every time Finn tries to catch a fly, he either succeeds (Success) or misses (Failure). If his success rate is always 70%, each single attempt is a Bernoulli trial.

section_2.title: The BINS Criteria
section_2.content: Define when a scenario qualifies as a Binomial Distribution using the BINS acronym: Binary (Success/Failure), Independent (one trial doesn't affect the next), Number (fixed number of trials 'n'), and Same probability 'p' for each trial. Use an animated checklist.
section_2.example: Finn decides to catch exactly 10 flies (Fixed Number). Each jump is independent, the outcome is only caught or not caught (Binary), and his skill stays at 70% (Same 'p').

section_3.title: The Mathematical Recipe (The Formula)
section_3.content: Break down the formula P(X=k) = nCk * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Use color-coding to link the math to the visual: nCk (the number of ways to arrange successes), p^k (probability of successes), and (1-p)^(n-k) (probability of failures).
section_3.example: To find the chance of Finn catching exactly 7 out of 10 flies, we calculate 10C7 (combinations of attempts) times 0.7 to the 7th power, times 0.3 to the 3rd power.

section_4.title: Visualizing the Distribution
section_4.content: Transition from a single calculation to a full probability histogram. Show how the shape changes based on 'p'. If p=0.5, it’s symmetric (like a bell curve); if p is high or low, the graph skews. Use an animated bar chart that 'grows' as we change the variables.
section_4.example: A histogram showing the probability of Finn catching 0, 1, 2... up to 10 flies. Since his success is high (0.7), the tallest bars on the graph will cluster around 7.

section_5.title: Application and Summary
section_5.content: Summarize the key takeaways: Binomial distributions help us predict outcomes in repeated trials. Mention real-world applications like quality control in factories or pharmaceutical testing.
section_5.example: A 'Quality Control Robot' checking a batch of 100 circuit boards for defects. If the defect rate is 2%, we use the Binomial distribution to predict the likelihood of finding more than 5 broken boards.

        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

                "- Formula: P(X=k) = (n choose k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k)"
